papers.abstract: Background: In postmastectomy radiotherapy, radiation reaches an already-reconstructed breast, and implant-based reconstruction remains feasible in selected patients. Far less studied is reconstruction within a previously irradiated field: after breast-conserving therapy, ipsilateral breast tumor recurrence (IBTR), and salvage mastectomy. We compared implant-based and autologous reconstruction in this setting and propose a hypothesis-generating treatment algorithm. Methods: From 2219 consecutive breast reconstructions (2012-2026), we cross-matched implant-removal, radiotherapy, and local-recurrence registries to identify all immediate total reconstructions of a previously irradiated breast after salvage mastectomy for IBTR (n = 13; 8 implant-based [all stand-alone, without vascularized flap coverage], 5 autologous [all latissimus dorsi-based]). The primary endpoint was reconstruction failure, defined in a modality-neutral manner as definitive loss or abandonment of the reconstruction; implant-based reconstructions of breasts not previously irradiated at the time of reconstruction (n = 689) served as a descriptive institutional reference cohort. Results: Seven of eight implants (87.5%) were removed at 3 to 51 months; the single retained implant has a persistent wound; none achieved complication-free success. Failure modes comprised early envelope necrosis, periprosthetic infection, and late attritional failure; chronic retained-capsule seroma followed removal without capsulectomy. All five autologous reconstructions healed without failure or unplanned reoperation (reconstruction failure, 7/8 [87.5%; 95% CI, 47.3-99.7%] vs. 0/5 [0%; 95% CI, 0-52.2%], p = 0.005; log-rank p = 0.039; median follow-up, 32.0 vs. 10.9 months; failure or major complication, 8/8 vs. 0/5, p = 0.0008). The implant-removal rate also exceeded that of the institutional reference cohort (87.5% vs. 11.2%; unadjusted, descriptive comparison). Conclusions: In this small consecutive series, stand-alone implant-based reconstruction of the previously irradiated breast was associated with a very high failure rate, whereas reconstruction importing well-vascularized autologous tissue healed in every case, a pattern biologically consistent with chronic radiation injury. These findings constitute a strong cautionary signal rather than definitive evidence. Our findings support an autologous-first approach after salvage mastectomy of the irradiated breast; stand-alone implant-based reconstruction should be offered only to carefully selected, fully counseled patients, and the proposed algorithm requires external validation.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) comprises distinct cellular states characterized by different differentiation programs and therapeutic responses. How a cell-surface receptor adapts its function across these states remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated whether the spatial organization and functional output of CD44 vary across PDAC cellular states. Methods: CD44 expression and spatial distribution were examined in human PDAC tissues and PDAC cell models representing different differentiation states. The functional roles of CD44 were investigated using genetic depletion, transcriptomic analysis, migration and invasion assays, and xenograft and orthotopic models. Hyaluronan (HA) responsiveness and downstream signaling were assessed following exogenous HA stimulation, and the therapeutic effects of HA synthesis inhibition with 4-methylumbelliferone (4-MU) were evaluated alone or in combination with gemcitabine. Results: In differentiated PDAC tissues and classical PDAC models, CD44 was predominantly localized to the basolateral membrane and spatially segregated from E-cadherin at cell-cell junctions, consistent with a role in epithelial organization and cell-matrix interactions. In contrast, poorly differentiated PDAC tissues and basal-like models exhibited increased CD44 abundance, E-cadherin loss, and redistribution of CD44 along the cell periphery. Genetic depletion of CD44 preferentially impaired malignant phenotypes in basal-like models. Mechanistically, basal-like cells exhibited enhanced CD44-dependent responsiveness to extracellular HA, accompanied by activation of EMT-associated signaling and destabilization of E-cadherin. Inhibition of HA synthesis with 4-MU preferentially suppressed basal-like PDAC models and enhanced gemcitabine sensitivity, with these effects further supported in orthotopic models. Conclusions: These findings suggest that the functional output of CD44 in PDAC is influenced not only by its expression level but also by cellular context and spatial organization. The context-dependent responsiveness of the HA-CD44 axis may contribute to functional heterogeneity among PDAC states and represents a potential therapeutic vulnerability of basal-like PDAC.

papers.abstract: Abstract Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) are clonal hematologic malignancies characterized by the overproduction of mature myeloid lineage cells. Although JAK2 inhibitors, such as ruxolitinib, can alleviate constitutional symptoms, they typically fail to eradicate malignant clones or reverse bone marrow fibrosis. Moreover, treatment failure and drug intolerance often limit their long-term use. Recent studies have identified PIM1 kinase as an important mediator of MPN pathogenesis. PIM1 expression is upregulated in MPN hematopoietic progenitors, which may contribute to aberrant proliferation and disease progression by regulating key downstream effectors, including mTORC1, BAD, MYC, HIF-1α, and TGF-β. Notably, PIM1 contributes to JAK2 inhibitor-persistent cell growth, and its inhibition restores ruxolitinib sensitivity in JAK2 mutant cells. Preclinical studies using genetic ablation and pharmacological inhibition of PIM1 have shown significant attenuation of the myelofibrosis phenotype in mouse models, providing a strong rationale for targeting this kinase. PIM kinase inhibitors are currently being evaluated in clinical trials for patients with myelofibrosis. This review summarizes the current understanding of PIM1 biology in the context of MPNs, details the molecular mechanisms underlying its pathogenic contributions, and evaluates the translational potential of PIM1-targeted therapies for MPNs.

papers.abstract: Abstract Image-guided ablation has emerged as a potentially curative treatment for colorectal cancer liver metastases (CRLM), yet substantial heterogeneity persists in patient selection, technical execution, and perioperative management. To establish standardized, evidence-based guidance, a multidisciplinary panel of 68 experts including image-guided interventionalists, surgeons, and oncologists conducted a systematic review of literature from 2000 to 2025 and developed consensus recommendations through a modified two-round Delphi process. Evidence was graded using the Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine framework, achieving at least conditional consensus (≥75% agreement) for all statements. Finally, twenty consensus recommendations were established addressing patient selection, imaging evaluation, image-guided techniques, ablation strategies, complication management, surveillance protocols, and combination therapies. This expert consensus provides a comprehensive framework for optimizing image-guided ablation as an integral component of multidisciplinary, personalized CRLM management.

papers.abstract: Abstract Background & Aims: Clinical responses to atezolizumab plus bevacizumab (AB) therapy can vary across hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) nodules among individual patients. This study aimed to derive and externally validate a non-invasive radiomics signature (ABRad) translated from a transcriptome signature for nodule-level prediction of AB response (ABS). Methods: We originally derived and validated ABS using 209 and 44 pre-treatment HCC samples from the IMbrave150 and GO30140 trials, respectively. ABS was then translated into ABRad using a machine-learning approach on 59 patients with paired genome-wide transcriptome and pre-resection computed tomography imaging from surgically resected HCC. Subsequently, ABRad was externally validated using 178 HCC nodules from 55 patients treated with AB therapy. Results: The 148-gene ABS predicted therapeutic response and progression-free survival (PFS) in the clinical trial cohorts. The final ABRad model, constructed using a random forest algorithm, was heavily weighted toward contrast-enhanced features. In the external validation cohort, ABRad demonstrated a significant positive association with the degree of therapeutic response (p <0.001). The areas under receiver operating characteristics curve for predicting complete response (CR), objective response (OR), and disease control (DC) were 0.71 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.61-0.80), 0.65 (95% CI, 0.56-0.73), and 0.69 (95% CI, 0.59-0.78), respectively. Nodule-level ABRad was independently associated with therapeutic response with adjusted odds ratios of 3.39 (95% CI, 1.40-8.21) for CR, 2.55 (95% CI, 1.19-5.67) for OR, and 2.60 (95% CI, 1.03-6.56) for DC. Patient-level ABRad was significantly associated with prolonged PFS (p = 0.005). Conclusions: ABRad successfully predicted nodule-level response to AB therapy in HCC.

papers.abstract: To establish baseline growth rates of lung nodules in untreated head and neck adenoid cystic carcinoma(ACC) patients and analyze associated clinical and molecular factors influencing these rates. CT was used to calculate the diameter of 74 pulmonary metastatic nodules in 37 patients under natural state. The diameter growth rate of lung metastatic nodules was fitted with a linear regression equation, and the differences in the progression rate of lung metastasis among patients were compared. Additionally, clinical features such as location, pathological subtypes, and staging were also collected to compare their correlation with the growth rate of lung metastatic nodules. Subsequently, single-cell sequencing data from three lung metastatic nodules of differing diameters within the same case were analyzed. We defined three different states based on the progression of lung metastases: rapid progression was defined as a monthly diameter increase of more than 1 mm in 16.2% (6/37) of the patients; slow progression was defined as a monthly diameter increase between 0.3-1 mm in 56.8% (21/37) of the patients; and stable state was defined as a monthly diameter increase of less than 0.3 mm in 27.0% (10/37) of the patients. In addition, factors such as low expression of TP63, a higher pathological grade (Grade III), and a nodule diameter greater than 10mm at initial diagnosis of lung metastasis were identified as significant predictors for a faster diameter growth rate (P<0.05). Subsequently, through single-cell sequencing analysis, it was found that rapidly progressing nodules exhibited upregulation of signals related to hypoxia, vascular genesis, and a weakening of immune response-related signals. The findings of this study suggest that baseline characteristics based on the growth rate of pulmonary metastatic nodules may be used to help stratify the progression rate of lung metastasis. In particular, based on our observations, for patients with pulmonary metastatic lesions presenting with a nodule diameter > 10 mm, pathological grade III, and low TP63 expression at initial diagnosis, clinicians might consider adopting closer follow-up monitoring or potentially initiating intervention measures earlier. Additionally, for rapidly growing pulmonary metastatic nodules, it may be worth considering targeted therapy against hypoxic/anti-angiogenic pathways or combination with immunotherapy aimed at restoring or enhancing local immune responses.

papers.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma remains among the most lethal solid tumors, with 5-year survival near 13% despite decades of incremental change, and current management continues to be organized around anatomic resectability and a chemotherapy backbone applied largely without regard to tumor biology. This article advances the thesis that the dominant paradigm underperforms because it treats a systemic, molecularly convergent, multi-compartment disease as though it were a local one. We first summarize the real advances of the past decade-in surgery, systemic therapy, molecular profiling, and immunotherapy-and then identify five interlocking failure points that persist despite them: (i) selection by vessel anatomy, judged on imaging criteria that are read inconsistently and that classify inaccurately even where read consistently, and applied to splanchnic veins without accounting for their baseline variability and tumor-associated thrombosis; (ii) occult metastasis and the resulting limits of local cure for the systemic majority, evidenced by the gap between complete resection and durable survival and by early distant recurrence; (iii) the addition of radiotherapy, which improves local control without extending survival; (iv) chemotherapy chosen without reference to a validated prognostic classical/basal-like distinction, although prospective subtype-directed regimen selection has not yet improved outcomes in randomized testing; and (v) a sequential, non-integrated structure in which systemic and immune therapy are deferred and no definitive path exists for the roughly 80% who are not surgical candidates. We then propose a multimodal, biology-guided framework that answers each failure point, with every component graded on an explicit evidence scale: corrected tumor-suppressor gene therapy matched to lesion type, a systemic backbone combining renin-angiotensin system-pathway inhibition with immunogenically sequenced chemotherapy and personalized neoantigen vaccination, in-situ immune conversion of an accessible tumor by cryoablation with local priming and natural killer (NK) cell delivery, and front-end biological patient selection. The framework is conceptual rather than product-specific; we specify its rationale, its integration in time, a staged first-in-human development program, and the studies required to test it. The objective is to convert local disease into systemic benefit-a step the current paradigm is not designed to take.

papers.abstract: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is characterized by VHL-HIF pathway alterations, lipid remodeling, abnormal angiogenesis, and marked immune heterogeneity. These features create a highly vascular yet unevenly perfused microenvironment in which vascular dysfunction, hypoxia, stromal barriers, and myeloid clearance influence whether cell death becomes immunologically productive. Although immune checkpoint inhibitor combinations, vascular endothelial growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and HIF-2α inhibitors have improved outcomes, primary and acquired resistance and discordant responses among lesions remain common. Bulk PD-L1 expression, immune-cell abundance, and cell-death-related transcript signatures do not resolve this heterogeneity. Following current nomenclature, regulated cell death (RCD) is the mechanistically preferred umbrella term; we retain programmed cell death (PCD) in the conceptual label because it remains widely used in the RCC oncology literature, while requiring RCD execution-level evidence for mechanistic claims. Single-cell and spatial multi-omics studies increasingly show that the identity of the dying cell, execution of the death program, accessibility of death-derived material, and the recipient immune cells operate as a coupled local system. We define a PCD-associated immune niche as a spatial tissue state in which representative, non-exclusive immune-routing axes can direct tumor-cell death toward cDC1-mediated cross-presentation and adaptive antitumor immunity, TAM-dominant efferocytosis and tissue repair, or intermediate mixed states. This Review focuses predominantly on ccRCC, evaluates ferroptosis, apoptosis, pyroptosis, necroptosis, and PANoptosis, and briefly considers emerging RCD modalities for which ccRCC evidence is less mature. We further propose composite spatial biomarkers and mechanism-guided combinations that link cellular source, execution evidence, immune routing, and clinical outcome.

papers.abstract: Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) represents a unique lymphoid malignancy characterized by the presence of rare malignant Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS) cells embedded within a highly complex and immunologically active tumor microenvironment. Over the past decade, advances in genomic and transcriptomic technologies have substantially refined the understanding of HL pathogenesis. Recurrent genetic alterations affecting key oncogenic pathways, including NF-κB, JAK/STAT, and PI3K/AKT signaling, cooperate with widespread mechanisms of immune evasion to sustain tumor cell survival and proliferation. Epstein-Barr virus infection contributes to lymphomagenesis in a significant subset of cases by providing surrogate survival signals, modulating immune interactions and targeting the telomere-shelterin complex through LMP1. In parallel, emerging evidence highlights the central role of the tumor microenvironment, which actively supports malignant cell growth through direct cellular interactions, cytokine signaling, and metabolic and immune-regulatory mechanisms. Recent studies using circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) profiling and single-cell approaches have enabled non-invasive genomic characterization and revealed biologically distinct molecular subgroups, further underscoring the interplay between tumor genetics and immune contexture. These insights are reshaping disease classification and opening new avenues for biomarker-driven therapeutic strategies. A deeper integration of molecular, immunological, and microenvironmental features will be crucial to optimize risk stratification and to develop more precise and less toxic treatments for patients with HL.

papers.abstract: Background: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have been shown to improve long term outcomes and pathological complete response (pCR) rates in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). However, treatment response remains heterogeneous. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has emerged as a promising noninvasive biomarker for predicting response to immunotherapy-containing treatment regimens. Purpose: To systematically review studies evaluating MRI biomarkers for predicting response to immunotherapy-containing treatment regimens in breast cancer. Methods: A PRISMA-guided systematic review of PubMed was performed for studies published between June 2019 and June 2026 evaluating MRI-based prediction of pCR or immunotherapy response in breast cancer. Data regarding study design, MRI techniques, predictive performance, and study characteristics were extracted and qualitatively synthesized. Results: Across the ten included studies, conventional MRI generally demonstrated moderate predictive performance (AUC 0.65-0.75), whereas multiparametric radiomics models achieved the highest predictive performance (AUC up to 0.88). Several consistent themes emerged. Studies evaluating neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy (NACI) reported increased MRI-pathology discordance and reduced reliability of enhancement-based assessment alone, suggesting that conventional MRI response assessment may require refinement in this treatment setting. Functional MRI biomarkers, including diffusion-weighted imaging and dynamic enhancement metrics, identified treatment response earlier than baseline morphologic imaging, while radiomics models integrating MRI with clinical or molecular biomarkers consistently demonstrated the strongest predictive performance. However, evidence remained limited by heterogeneous imaging protocols, small study populations, and limited external validation. Conclusions: MRI, particularly multiparametric and radiomics-enhanced approaches, is evolving beyond conventional morphologic assessment to provide complementary information regarding tumor biology and treatment response in patients undergoing NACI. However, standardized imaging protocols and prospective multicenter validation are needed before MRI-derived biomarkers can be incorporated into routine clinical decision-making.

papers.abstract: Rare cancers represent a substantial health burden, comprising 25% of cancer mortality. Early-phase oncology trials are essential for rare cancers, where limited patient numbers, biological heterogeneity, and the absence of established standards of care necessitate innovative approaches to drug development. Advances in trial design-including basket, umbrella, and adaptive platforms-have enabled efficient evaluation of molecularly defined subgroups and accelerated identification of clinically meaningful activity across rare tumor types. Early-phase studies have demonstrated the therapeutic potential of antibody-drug conjugates, immunotherapy, targeted agents, and cellular therapies, particularly when guided by predictive biomarkers and tumor-agnostic strategies. These approaches have expanded treatment options for patients with historically limited therapeutic opportunities. Persistent challenges remain, including restricted trial access, difficulties with patient accrual, variability in biomarker assessment, and uncertainty regarding generalizability of outcomes. Additional challenges persist after early-phase trial completion, as continued access to therapies demonstrating clinical benefit may remain limited when regulatory approval or broader clinical availability has not yet been established. Evolving regulatory and collaborative frameworks have partially mitigated these barriers by supporting multi-institutional enrollment and pathway-flexible approvals. Over the past decade, biomarker-driven strategies have been increasingly incorporated into modern clinical trial design, shifting the field away from traditional histology-based approaches. Continued innovation in trial design, biomarker integration, and collaborative infrastructure will be essential to sustaining progress and expanding durable clinical benefit for patients with rare cancers.

papers.abstract: Platinum-based chemotherapy remains a key treatment for epithelial ovarian cancer, but platinum resistance is a major cause of treatment failure and mortality. Traditionally, platinum resistance has been defined by the interval between the last platinum treatment and disease progression, with progression within six months generally classified as platinum-resistant. This six-month platinum-free interval has long provided a useful framework for treatment selection. However, growing preclinical and clinical evidence suggests that this interval should not be treated as a strict biological boundary. Platinum susceptibility can change as tumors evolve, with some tumors retaining residual sensitivity while others develop stable or potentially modifiable resistance mechanisms. These mechanisms include restoration of homologous recombination, altered DNA-damage tolerance, epigenetic regulation, changes in platinum transport and detoxification, adaptive survival signaling, and alterations in cell-death pathways. Some resistance mechanisms are relatively stable, whereas others may remain biologically plastic and potentially amenable to therapeutic modification. This distinction has important implications for platinum rechallenge. Responses to platinum reintroduction in selected patients previously classified as platinum-resistant indicate that the six-month interval does not fully capture the biology of platinum responsiveness. However, renewed clinical activity after rechallenge should not automatically be interpreted as biological resensitization. True resensitization requires evidence that a defined resistance mechanism has been modified and that this alteration increases platinum susceptibility. Preclinical studies have identified multiple strategies to modify platinum-resistance pathways, but clinical translation remains limited. This perspective therefore proposes that platinum resistance should be understood as a clinically defined phenotype encompassing biologically heterogeneous states, some of which may be stable and others potentially reversible. Recognizing this distinction has implications for biomarker development, treatment selection, trial design, and interpretation of platinum rechallenge. Prospective studies incorporating longitudinal tumor profiling and functional assessments of platinum susceptibility may ultimately identify patients in whom platinum activity can be therapeutically restored.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: The incidence of small intestinal neuroendocrine tumors (SI-NETs) has increased in recent years, while effective therapeutic options remain limited. This study aimed to investigate the antitumor effects of orlistat on SI-NETs and elucidate the underlying mechanisms. Methods: The effects of orlistat were evaluated using STC-1 cells, patient-derived primary SI-NET cells, and xenograft models. Functional assays, RNA sequencing, lipidomic profiling, ATAC sequencing, and molecular analyses were performed to assess tumor-related phenotypes and investigate the underlying mechanisms. Results: Orlistat inhibited cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, induced G1-phase arrest and apoptosis, and suppressed tumor growth in vivo. Mechanistically, orlistat triggered endoplasmic reticulum stress, inhibited PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling, and upregulated activating transcription factor 3 (ATF3). Lipidomic profiling revealed alterations in lipid metabolism. Increased reactive oxygen species and lipid peroxidation, together with changes in ferroptosis-related proteins, indicated the involvement of ferroptosis-associated pathways. ATF3 overexpression reproduced the antitumor and ferroptosis-associated effects of orlistat. Integrated ATAC-seq and RNA-seq analyses identified CHAC1 as a potential downstream effector of ATF3. Conversely, ATF3 knockdown reduced CHAC1 expression and attenuated the effects of orlistat both in vitro and in vivo. Conclusions: Orlistat suppresses SI-NET progression and is associated with changes in endoplasmic reticulum stress, ATF3 expression, and ferroptosis-related responses, with CHAC1 identified as a potential downstream effector of ATF3. These findings support further investigation of orlistat as a potential therapeutic strategy for SI-NETs.

papers.abstract: Cellular senescence is a stress-induced, stable proliferative arrest that acts as a potent barrier to tumorigenesis, yet the senescence-associated secretory phenotype that accompanies it can paradoxically fuel inflammation, angiogenesis and the phenotypic plasticity contributing to tumor heterogeneity, therapy resistance and cancer stem cell emergence. A largely unexplored molecular layer in the senescence program is alternative pre-mRNA splicing, which generates protein isoforms with functionally divergent effects on cell-cycle arrest, apoptosis and the secretory program. More than 90% of human multi-exon genes are alternatively spliced, so most of the nearly 1000 genes linked to senescence are expected to produce several isoforms, yet fewer than twenty have been examined at this level, and direct evidence is available for only about half of these. We review how alternative splicing, together with related mechanisms such as alternative promoter usage and alternative reading-frame selection, modulates distinct outputs of the senescence program, including commitment, persistence, escape and SASP composition, across gene groups such as the TP53/TP63/TP73 family, MDM2/MDM4 and the androgen receptor locus. This evidence ranges from direct causal manipulation to correlative or mechanistically adjacent findings, classified explicitly by evidence level. Direct causal evidence remains limited, making isoform-resolved functional validation a major unmet need in the field.

papers.abstract: Background/objective: Multiple myeloma (MM) is a hematological malignancy characterized by the proliferation of clonal plasma cells. While [18F]FDG PET/CT is widely established for assessing disease extent, bone involvement, and treatment response in MM, novel molecular imaging targets like CXCR4 (e.g., using [68Ga]Ga-Pentixafor) have emerged to offer potentially superior sensitivity and theranostic applications. The aim of this manuscript is to systematically review and compare the diagnostic performance, expressed as detection rates, of CXCR4-targeted PET/CT versus [18F]FDG PET/CT in patients with MM. Methods: A systematic literature search was conducted across major databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library) for head-to-head comparative studies evaluating both [18F]FDG and [68Ga]Ga-Pentixafor PET/CT in MM patients. Risk of bias and study quality were assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool. Results: Eleven studies were collected, amounting to a total of 347 patients. A patient-based analysis showed that [68Ga]Ga-Pentixafor had a higher detection rate than [18F]FDG PET/CT (86.3%, 95% CI: 80.3-92.3% vs 60.9%, 95% CI: 42.5-79.4%). In a descriptive analysis, mean lesion SUVmax values reported across individual studies were generally higher with [68Ga]Ga-Pentixafor PET/CT than with [18F]FDG PET/CT. Conclusions: [68Ga]Ga-Pentixafor PET/CT may serve as a robust alternative or complementary imaging modality to [18F]FDG PET/CT in MM. It could also be helpful for selection in CXCR4-directed theranostic pathways, but more high-quality studies are warranted.

papers.abstract: Real-world evidence describing the presentation, management, and outcomes of follicular lymphoma (FL) in Saudi Arabia remains limited, and the frequency and prognostic weight of progression of disease within 24 months of first-line therapy (POD24) have not been reported in this population. This study evaluated the clinicopathological characteristics, treatment patterns, POD24 incidence, and survival outcomes of patients with FL treated at two Saudi tertiary centres. This two-centre retrospective chart review included adults with histologically confirmed FL diagnosed between November 1999 and May 2025. Overall survival (OS) and first-line progression-free survival (PFS) were measured from the initiation of first-line treatment and estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. POD24 was defined as progression, relapse, or death from any cause within 24 months of first-line initiation among patients evaluable for that endpoint. Outcomes were additionally examined by calendar era of diagnosis. All group comparisons were unadjusted and exploratory. A total of 139 patients were included. The mean age at diagnosis was 54.7 years (range, 18-91), 61.9% were male, 79.1% had Ann Arbor stage III-IV disease, and 51.1% had an FLIPI score ≥ 3. Bendamustine plus rituximab was the most frequent first-line regimen (43.9%), followed by R-CHOP (30.2%). The overall response rate was 77.0% in the whole cohort and 82.4% among the 125 patients who received response-evaluable systemic first-line therapy. After a median follow-up of 71.0 months, 5-year OS was 92.5% (95% CI, 84.8-96.4) and 5-year PFS was 66.1% (95% CI, 54.9-75.0); the corresponding medians were 210.0 and 114.6 months but were estimated with few patients at risk and should be interpreted cautiously. Among 97 patients evaluable for POD24, the event occurred in 24 (24.7%; 95% CI, 17.2-34.2), and the incidence was stable across calendar eras (23.4% before 2018 versus 24.5% thereafter; p = 1.000). Primary refractory disease accounted for 14 of the 24 events (58.3%). POD24 was associated with poorer ECOG performance status (odds ratio [OR] 11.08; 95% CI, 3.85-31.86), older age (OR 5.27; 95% CI, 2.00-13.89), and higher FLIPI score (OR 3.09; 95% CI, 1.13-8.42). In the 24-month landmark analysis, OS was significantly shorter after POD24 (log-rank p = 0.008), and both documented histological transformations occurred in the POD24 group. Patients with FL in this two-centre Saudi cohort frequently presented with advanced-stage and high-risk disease, yet contemporary anti-CD20-based treatment was associated with favourable long-term survival. Approximately one quarter of evaluable patients experienced POD24, predominantly as primary refractory disease, and this event identified a subgroup with materially inferior subsequent survival. POD24 may help identify patients who warrant closer surveillance and consideration for clinical trials or novel therapies.

papers.abstract: Locoregional therapies are used across the hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) treatment spectrum, including for curative treatment of small tumors, as bridging or downstaging therapy before liver transplant, for treatment of intermediate-stage disease, and as part of combination treatment with systemic therapy in selected patients. This narrative review summarizes recent developments in transarterial radioembolization (TARE), transarterial chemoembolization (TACE), and percutaneous ablation techniques and separates established clinical advances from early investigational work. The strongest evidence supports personalized TARE dosimetry and radiation segmentectomy, selective TACE with reassessment before repeat treatment, and image-guided thermal ablation with objective margin assessment. Phase 3 trials of TACE combined with antiangiogenic and immune checkpoint therapy demonstrated improved progression-free survival in selected patients with unresectable, nonmetastatic HCC, although the survival benefit of these combinations so far extends only to progression-free survival, and the best treatment sequence remains to be defined. Histotripsy, pulsed electric-field ablation, electrochemotherapy, cryoablation, high-intensity focused ultrasound, imageable or alternative radioembolic microspheres, new embolic agents, robotics, and artificial intelligence remain at different stages of clinical development. Most supporting data are derived from single-arm studies, retrospective cohort studies, trials in mixed liver-tumor populations, or studies in preclinical models. Treatment selection should account for tumor burden and location, liver function, portal hypertension, vascular invasion, transplant candidacy, available alternatives, local expertise, and patient preferences. Future studies should focus on durable local control, preservation of liver function, quality of life, transplant eligibility, overall survival, and cost.

papers.abstract: To compare the efficacy, survival benefits, and safety of whole-brain radiotherapy (WBRT) alone versus WBRT combined with simultaneous integrated boost (WBRT+SIB) for patients with brain metastases. A total of 100 patients treated from 2017 to 2022 were retrospectively analyzed. Tumor response was assessed per RECIST 1.1. Survival differences were compared using the Kaplan-Meier method and log-rank test. Multivariate Cox regression and subgroup analyses were performed to evaluate the prognostic value and stability of WBRT+SIB. The WBRT+SIB group exhibited numerically higher objective response and disease control rates without statistical significance. With a median follow-up of 31.0 months, WBRT+SIB significantly prolonged median overall survival (11.0 vs. 8.0 months, p = 0.011) and improved 1-, 2-, and 3-year survival rates. After adjusting for multiple confounders, WBRT+SIB independently reduced mortality risk (HR = 0.51, 95% CI: 0.27-0.97, p = 0.039). Subgroup analyses were exploratory; therefore, consistent survival advantages across strata cannot be confirmed. No significant differences in acute, subacute, or late neurotoxicity, including radiation-induced brain necrosis, were found between the two groups. WBRT+SIB was associated with longer overall survival compared with WBRT alone, without a significant increase in the incidence of radiotherapy-related adverse events. Although ORR and DCR were numerically higher in the WBRT+SIB group, these differences were not statistically significant. Given the limitations of this exploratory study, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and require validation in prospective randomized trials.

papers.abstract: Objective: To evaluate the incremental predictive value of pretreatment tri-modal ultrasound deep learning integrating two-dimensional ultrasound (2DUS), color Doppler flow imaging (CDFI), and contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) for predicting breast pathologic complete response (bpCR) after neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC), and to assess performance stability across independent centers. Methods: This retrospective multicenter study included 1089 patients with primary invasive breast cancer. Center 1 provided the training cohort (n = 572) and internal validation cohort (n = 246), whereas centers 2 (n = 160) and 3 (n = 111) served as independent external validation cohorts. Using pretreatment 2DUS, CDFI, and CEUS within a standardized intratumoral and 10-mm peritumoral framework, single-modality, all three dual-modality combinations, and tri-modal models were developed. The best-performing dual-modality model was identified and locked during training as the primary imaging comparator. A Tri-modal + Clinical model further integrated pretreatment clinical and biomarker variables. Performance was assessed using AUC, Brier score, calibration, decision curve analysis, and ablation experiments. Results: Overall, 383 patients (35.2%) achieved bpCR. CEUS was the strongest single modality, and 2DUS + CEUS was the best-performing dual-modality model. Compared with 2DUS + CEUS, the tri-modal model increased the AUC from 0.895 to 0.919 in the combined external cohort (ΔAUC, +0.023; 95% CI, +0.010 to +0.038; p = 0.001), with corresponding improvements in Brier score (0.124 to 0.105) and F1 score (0.747 to 0.786). The AUC point estimate increased in both external centers, although the 95% CI for the incremental AUC included zero in external validation cohort 2. Despite modest standalone discrimination, CDFI provided measurable incremental information when added to 2DUS + CEUS. Further integration of pretreatment clinical and biomarker variables increased the combined external AUC to 0.935. Reduced-input retraining showed performance decreases after omission of any modality, with the largest reduction after CEUS omission. Conclusions: Pretreatment tri-modal ultrasound deep learning provided incremental predictive value for bpCR beyond the best dual-modality model, with a consistent direction of benefit across two independent external centers. Clinical and biomarker integration provided additional predictive information, supporting further evaluation of this multimodal framework for individualized pretreatment bpCR prediction.

papers.abstract: Gastric cancer remains a leading cause of cancer mortality. However, earlier detection has increased the number of cases suitable for organ-preserving treatment. Sentinel node navigation surgery has been proposed as an alternative to standard gastrectomy for early gastric cancer. The safety of this procedure hinges on how accurately sentinel node mapping predicts nodal status. This systematic review synthesizes its diagnostic accuracy and outcome data. We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, the Web of Science Core Collection, and Scopus from inception without date limits, along with two trial registries; screening was restricted to English-language reports. Estimates and exact binomial (Clopper-Pearson) 95% confidence intervals were recalculated from each study's reported contingency counts using a consistent statistical method. Each included cohort was appraised using QUADAS-2. Eight cohorts contributed per-patient accuracy data, and three contributed per-node molecular comparisons. Detection rates were 97.1% or higher in every cohort entry, with the exception of the naked-eye dye arm of a within-cohort comparison and the smallest feasibility series. Sensitivity was 93.0% (53/57; 95% CI, 83.0-98.1) in the single adequately powered treatment-naive cohort, compared to 69.6% (16/23; 47.1-86.8) in the single prospective trial conducted after non-curative endoscopic resection. Sensitivity also depended on the thoroughness of sentinel node examination: within one cohort, the same patients yielded a sensitivity of 53.6% with single-plane frozen section versus 85.7% with multiple paraffin sections. Therefore, estimates were not pooled. No appraised cohort demonstrated a low risk of bias across all four QUADAS-2 domains. Stomach preservation guided by sentinel node mapping may be a reasonable approach for treatment-naive disease in experienced centers. However, it is not supported after non-curative endoscopic resection.

papers.abstract: Background: Maternal embryonic leucine zipper kinase (MELK) is a cell cycle-regulated serine/threonine kinase frequently overexpressed in human malignancies, and represents a promising anticancer drug target. Discovery of structurally novel, highly selective MELK inhibitors remains an unmet need. Methods: In the study, we implemented an integrated computational pipeline combining four machine learning regressors (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM), hierarchical Glide docking (HTVS to SP to XP), MM/GBSA rescoring, ADMET prediction, and 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations to screen a ~15.58 million-compound commercial library, yielding 12 prioritized candidates. Three commercially available compounds (CPD4, CPD6, CPD10) were evaluated in an antiproliferative panel. Results: CPD6 was identified as the most active hit, with IC50 values of 1.44 μM in MDA-MB-468 and 1.66 μM in H1299, modestly exceeding the reference compound MELK-8a under the same assay conditions (2.48 and 2.51 μM, respectively). Cellular thermal shift assay in cell lysates provided biochemical evidence of MELK engagement, and 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations supported a computationally predicted binding mode in the MELK kinase domain. Additional substrate phosphorylation and MELK overexpression rescue assays further supported MELK-dependent inhibitory activity. Colony formation, EdU incorporation, and cell cycle analyses demonstrated dose-dependent antiproliferative effects and G2/M arrest, with concomitant downregulation of CDC25C, CDK1, and Cyclin B1. Discussion: CPD6 is a structurally novel MELK lead distinct from reported inhibitors. While our data support MELK target engagement, kinome selectivity profiling remains required, and this ML pipeline demonstrates the utility of AI-driven large-scale anticancer lead screening. Conclusions: Using the integrated machine-learning virtual screening pipeline established in this work, we identified CPD6 as a structurally novel MELK-targeted lead that engages MELK, induces G2/M arrest, and exerts low-micromolar antiproliferative activity in triple-negative breast cancer and lung adenocarcinoma models.

papers.abstract: Oligometastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is defined anatomically by a threshold of five or fewer metastatic lesions across three or fewer organs. That definition is a proxy for a biological question it cannot answer: whether the metastatic process has been arrested at a stage where eradication of all detectable disease is curative. Randomized phase II trials of local consolidative therapy have shown median progression-free survival gains of 6.2 and 8.0 months and, in one trial, a median overall survival of 41.2 months vs. 17.0 months, yet median progression-free survival with local therapy did not exceed 14.2 months, and the phase II/III NRG-LU002 trial found no significant survival benefit from adding local therapy to maintenance therapy. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) measures molecular disease burden. In resectable NSCLC, preoperative ctDNA detection is associated with a higher risk of relapse; in oligometastatic disease, the baseline sample is instead the quantitative reference for response. ctDNA kinetics during induction therapy track systemic response before any operation, although no response threshold has been validated, and postoperative molecular residual disease anticipates radiological relapse by a median of approximately 5 months. This review synthesizes the evidence linking liquid biopsy to surgical decision-making and proposes, as a hypothesis for prospective testing, a dynamic risk stratification framework anchored on five plasma sampling points. We separate established prognostic evidence from untested hypotheses, address oncogene-driven and other oligometastatic states, and define the assay requirements, confounders and trial designs needed before ctDNA can select patients for or against thoracic resection.

papers.abstract: Neoadjuvant treatment for early-stage triple-negative breast cancer has been widely used, and the KEYNOTE-522 (KN522) regimen has become a standard of care for early-stage TNBC, with alternative treatment options including a dose-dense anthracycline/taxane-based regimen for patients without access to neoadjuvant immunotherapy. Nevertheless, real-world evidence in Chinese populations, especially high-risk cohorts such as older populations and those with substantial nodal burden, is limited regarding both efficacy and tolerability. This study describes the outcomes associated with neoadjuvant systemic therapy in a Hong Kong Chinese cohort. This study aimed to describe the feasibility, treatment delivery, tolerability and safety of the KN522 regimen in stage I-III TNBC in a Chinese cohort in Hong Kong. Another cohort treated with dose-dense neoadjuvant chemotherapy, which is also a standard-of-care treatment alternative, is presented to provide context of local treatment practice. We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study of 59 patients with stage I-III TNBC who received neoadjuvant systemic treatment prior to breast surgery at a tertiary centre in Hong Kong between February 2022 and June 2025. The primary cohort received the KN522 regimen (n = 30). A contextual reference cohort received dose-dense epirubicin/cyclophosphamide followed by paclitaxel (n = 29) to describe local treatment patterns. Descriptive outcomes included pathological complete response (pCR), treatment delivery, adverse events, surgery completion, and exploratory event-free survival (EFS). Analyses were primarily descriptive; between-cohort comparisons were exploratory in nature. Fifty-nine patients were included overall: 30 treated with the KN522 regimen and 29 treated with dose-dense neoadjuvant chemotherapy. In the KN522 cohort, the median age was 56 years, 80.0% of patients were postmenopausal, and 33.3% had N3 disease. Pathological complete response occurred in 13 of 30 patients (43.3%; exact 95% CI 25.5-62.6%). Grade ≥3 chemotherapy-related adverse events occurred in 15 patients (50.0%), immune-related adverse events occurred in 11 patients (36.6%), and Grade 3 or higher immune-related adverse events occurred in four patients (13.3%). Pembrolizumab was suspended in six patients (20.0%), while all 30 patients proceeded to definitive surgery. In the dose-dense chemotherapy cohort, the pCR rate was 31.0%, with a grade ≥3 chemotherapy-related adverse event rate of 20.7%, and all patients proceeded to definitive surgery. In this descriptive real-world single-centre Hong Kong study, the neoadjuvant KN522 regimen was feasible in Chinese patients with early TNBC, although treatment-related toxicity and treatment modification were common. The observed pCR rate was lower than that reported in the original KN522 trial, possibly reflecting differences in patient selection and real-world treatment delivery patterns. Larger multi-centre studies are needed to evaluate outcomes in Chinese and other Asian populations.

papers.abstract: Cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD) can compromise cardiovascular health and the delivery of anticancer treatment. Echocardiography and cardiac biomarkers remain the first-line surveillance tools; cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) provides complementary assessment of ventricular function and myocardial tissue when findings are inconclusive or additional characterization may change management. This narrative review examines multiparametric CMR across seven anticancer treatment groups and proposes a risk-adapted approach to its clinical use. Cine imaging, T1 and T2 mapping, extracellular volume fraction (ECV), late gadolinium enhancement, and feature-tracking strain provide different, partly overlapping information. Serial interpretation requires attention to local reference ranges, measurement reproducibility, hematocrit, and acquisition and analysis consistency. An absolute ECV increase of at least 3 percentage points is discussed as an observational risk signal, not proof of collagen deposition or a validated treatment threshold. The guideline threshold of a greater than 15% relative decline in global longitudinal strain derives from echocardiography and should not be assumed to apply directly to CMR feature tracking. We distinguish guideline-supported practice, randomized evidence, observational evidence, and mechanistic extrapolation from the authors' proposed surveillance and rechallenge framework. Suspected immune checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis requires urgent clinical evaluation even when CMR is negative. Prospective trials are needed to establish whether CMR-informed management improves cardiovascular outcomes, treatment completion, or survival.

papers.abstract: Platinum-based chemotherapy remains a standard-of-care treatment for non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet its efficacy is influenced by multiple factors, such as the functionality of DNA damage response pathways. DNA-damaging agents, like cisplatin, contribute to the generation of an "inflamed" tumor microenvironment (TME), which in turn correlates with an active antitumor immune response. MicroRNAs (miRNAs), a family of small, non-coding RNAs, have emerged as critical post-transcriptional regulators of gene expression, playing vital roles in modulating DNA Damage Repair (DDR) pathways and sensitivity to cisplatin. Their functional involvement in these mechanisms underscores their potential as diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers in lung cancer. In this study, we investigated the diagnostic and prognostic value of a previously validated six-miRNA signature (hsa-miR-26a, hsa-miR-29c, hsa-miR-34a, hsa-miR-30-5p, hsa-miR-30e-3p and hsa-miR-497) in paired tumor and healthy tissue samples from surgically treated NSCLC patients (n = 76), who later received platinum-based therapy. To explore the translational applicability of this signature, we also compared miRNA expression levels between matched tumor tissue and plasma samples (n = 36). We further examined the presence of an "inflamed" TME and its association with the miRNA signature by examining the mRNA levels of TIGIT, CD8A, FOXP3, CXCL10 and PD-L1, and performing correlation analysis. All selected miRNAs were significantly downregulated in NSCLC tumor tissue compared to healthy samples. Moreover, miRNA expression was differentially regulated in plasma samples, supporting their potential clinical relevance as minimally invasive biomarkers. The complete six-miRNA signature demonstrated good discriminatory ability between tumor and matched non-malignant tissue (AUC = 0.786, 95% CI: 0.713-0.860; p < 0.001), with 72% sensitivity and 77.3% specificity. A significant correlation with relapse-free survival (RFS) (p = 0.039) was also observed. Distinct immune-related transcriptional alterations were observed in tumor tissue, including increased expression of immune checkpoint-associated genes (TIGIT and PD-L1) and reduced CD8A expression. Tumor PD-L1 expression showed modest positive correlations with miR-26a (p = 0.046) and miR-30e-3p (p = 0.031). Our findings underscore the potential value of this novel six-miRNA signature both as a prognostic and diagnostic biomarker in NSCLC. Its correlation with immune microenvironment characteristics supports its relevance in guiding personalized therapeutic strategies. This signature warrants further clinical validation and may serve as a valuable tool for patient stratification and outcome prediction for patients treated with platinum-based chemotherapy.

papers.abstract: PM is a locally aggressive tumor associated with asbestos exposure. Despite legislative efforts to regulate asbestos use, its incidence continues to rise in some parts of the world. Chemotherapy and immunotherapy have improved survival in PM patients, but overall survival remains poor. MTAP loss is frequent in PM and may influence tumor behavior, resulting in a poorer prognosis. MTAP-deficient tumors exhibit unique metabolic vulnerabilities that have stimulated the development of targeted therapeutic strategies in recent years with promising results. The aim of this review is to analyze the prognostic and predictive value of MTAP in PM patients, as well as the outcomes of drugs with potential activity against this target.

papers.abstract: Background: Maximal safe resection remains the cornerstone of glioma surgery, particularly in eloquent regions where oncologic gain must be balanced against functional preservation. While 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA) fluorescence-guided surgery improves extent of resection in high-grade gliomas under general anesthesia, its role during awake craniotomy (AC) remains underdeveloped. We aimed to evaluate the oncologic and functional outcomes of 5-ALA-guided tumor resection during AC. Methods: PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception to February 2026 for studies reporting original data on AC using 5-ALA following PRISMA guidelines. Results: Across ten studies comprising 108 patients, fluorescence positivity was 79.2% in high-grade gliomas (Grade III-IV) and 24.1% in low-grade gliomas (Grade II), among the 83 patients with both grade and fluorescence data available (grade was not reported for 19 patients in one case series, and 6 patients in one cohort study did not receive 5-ALA and were excluded from grade- and fluorescence-stratified analyses). Gross total resection was achieved in 62.2% of patients with evaluable extent-of-resection data (56.5% of the full cohort), reaching 66.7% in the largest comparative cohort. Transient aphasia occurred in 32.6% of evaluable patients, while permanent aphasia and persistent hemiparesis were observed in 14.6% and 16.9%, respectively. In multiple studies, resection was intentionally halted despite persistent fluorescence when functional mapping identified an eloquent cortex, underscoring that mapping remained the decisive determinant of surgical boundaries. No study reported conversion to general anesthesia. Conclusions: 5-ALA-guided resection during AC appears feasible and clinically useful, particularly for high-grade gliomas in eloquent regions. Permanent neurological morbidity was observed in a minority of patients, within a range broadly consistent with awake glioma surgery generally, but the absence of a non-5-ALA comparator group means that functional safety relative to awake mapping alone cannot yet be established with confidence. Across the available literature, 5-ALA consistently enhances intraoperative tumor visualization, supports identification of residual fluorescent disease, and integrates well with cortical and subcortical mapping without clear evidence of increased permanent neurological morbidity. Although functional mapping remains the decisive determinant of the final resection boundary, the available evidence supports 5-ALA as a valuable complementary adjunct in onco-functional glioma surgery.

papers.abstract: Giant keratinocyte carcinomas, comprising basal cell carcinoma (BCC) and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) with a maximum diameter ≥ 5 cm, pose substantial clinical challenges. This structured narrative review distinguishes giant-specific findings from contextual evidence in advanced or high-risk disease. The synthesis uses a retained bibliography assembled from searches described in earlier drafts as covering PubMed/MEDLINE and PubMed Central from January 2015 to March 2026, supplemented by citation and guideline searching and a focused update reported through 4 September 2026. A record-level search and screening log is unavailable; historical selection counts cannot be independently reconstructed. The review protocol was not registered, and exhaustive coverage or full PRISMA compliance is not claimed. Sources were classified by design and directness, with descriptive consideration of methodological limitations. The retained set contains 51 sources: nine containing direct giant-specific clinical evidence and 42 providing contextual evidence. Direct evidence consists principally of case reports, retrospective or comparative studies and a giant-cSCC literature synthesis. It links giant BCC with prolonged lesion duration, ulceration, deeper invasion and reconstructive burden. Giant-cSCC outcomes vary substantially between reported series. Evidence for Hedgehog-pathway inhibition, PD-1 blockade and most molecular mechanisms derives mainly from conventional or advanced disease. Management requires multidisciplinary assessment integrating size, pathological risk, resectability and patient factors. Giant-specific molecular and therapeutic evidence remains limited, and contextual treatment effects should not be interpreted as effects established specifically in tumours ≥ 5 cm.

papers.abstract: CD19-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has transformed the treatment of relapsed/refractory large B-cell lymphoma (r/r LBCL), yet primary resistance and relapse remain common. We evaluated how recent clinical and translational evidence refines established resistance frameworks and which knowledge gaps prevent the relative contribution of individual mechanisms from being determined. We conducted a structured narrative review of 14 selected clinical and translational studies addressing tumor-, product-, host-, and microenvironment-related dimensions of treatment failure, synthesized across four interpretive domains and compared with nine previous reviews. Durable benefit was associated with favorable tumor and immune transcriptional programs and greater CAR T-cell fitness, expansion, or persistence. Treatment failure was associated with tumor-intrinsic resistance programs, exhausted T-cell states, systemic inflammatory signals, and suppressive tumor-microenvironment features, including PD-L1-expressing macrophages. Antigen escape remained relevant, but incomplete serial CD19 assessment precluded conclusions about its relative contribution. Comparison with earlier reviews showed continuity rather than replacement, with LBCL-focused evidence adding biological resolution. Resistance and relapse after CD19 CAR T-cell therapy in LBCL are multifactorial. Prospective longitudinal studies integrating tumor tissue, apheresis and manufactured products, peripheral blood, and matched relapse samples are needed to validate predictive biomarkers and guide rational treatment strategies.

papers.abstract: Metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has historically been managed with systemic therapy, and local therapies have, in general, been avoided in the absence of symptoms directly related to a specific metastasis. Even if a specific site of disease, such as a local recurrence, had the potential to cause symptoms in the future, there was a bias against prophylactic palliation. It was well-established that most patients die of systemic progression. This approach is now under pressure from four directions. Retrospective case series have reported survival durations longer than anticipated in highly selected patients with low-volume, single-organ disease. A randomized phase II trial reported that metastasis-directed therapy prolonged progression-free survival. Biologic data indicate that the site of metastatic relapse is encoded in gene expression profiles already present in the primary tumor. Second-line systemic therapy has become substantially more effective, which lengthens the interval over which control of an untreated metastasis may become clinically important. We trace the oligometastatic concept from the 1995 Hellman and Weichselbaum hypothesis to the 2026 OligoPanc consensus definition of up to three lesions confined to a single organ, examine the criteria proposed for patient selection, summarize the surgical and ablative radiotherapy literature, and consider the trials that will determine whether this is a treatable disease state or a favorable prognostic phenotype. We conclude that induction systemic therapy, followed by response assessment that weighs the absence of disease progression, Carbohydrate Antigen 19-9 (CA19-9) kinetics, and performance status, is a defensible route to local therapy directed at the metastases and the primary tumor, and warrants prospective study.

papers.abstract: Reliable and reproducible imaging-response assessment is essential for endpoint evaluation in glioblastoma clinical trials. The Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology (RANO) criteria provide a rule-based framework for standardisation, but their implementation can still yield variable outputs between readers and across timepoints and trial sites. This partly reflects differences in lesion definition, measurement geometry, longitudinal tracking, and new-lesion adjudication. We externally evaluated an automated pipeline for auditable, RANO 2.0-aligned imaging-only response assessment using pre-existing segmentation masks. This retrospective feasibility and pilot evaluation used longitudinal glioblastoma magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies from the public single-centre LUMIERE dataset. Dataset-provided tumour segmentation masks were retained unchanged. An expert neuroradiologist visually reviewed the masks against the corresponding MRI images, and timepoints with segmentations clearly non-representative of tumour tissue were excluded. Deterministic rule-based processing performed lesion definition, admissibility-filtered measurement extraction, longitudinal tracking, new-lesion detection, and provisional response classification. Expert RANO imaging annotations and bidimensional measurements served as comparators rather than complete clinical RANO 2.0 adjudications. Analyses assessed agreement in the sum of products of diameters (SPD), longitudinal burden change, response classification, progression timing, new-lesion agreement, and failure modes, with patient-level clustered bootstrap resampling. Visual segmentation quality control excluded 57 timepoints across 42 patients, leaving 542 evaluable timepoints, including 506 matched to expert annotations. Across 84 expert-measured timepoints from 47 patients, the constrained maximum product of perpendicular diameters (Max-PPD-c) correlated with expert SPD (Pearson r = 0.753; Spearman ρ = 0.861), although the concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) was 0.680 and the median absolute percentage difference was 36.8%. Overall, 73.8% of measurements were within ±50% of expert SPD. Across 31 consecutive pairs from 17 patients, correlations for longitudinal percentage change were r = 0.715 and ρ = 0.874. Per-timepoint four-class response agreement was 48.1% (κ = 0.173), whereas final-timepoint binary progressive disease (PD) agreement was 76.0%. Among patients with PD by both methods, the pipeline assigned PD earlier more often than later, although the median timing difference was 0.0 weeks and the paired comparison was not statistically significant (p = 0.068). New-lesion detection had a positive predictive value (PPV) of 22.3% and negative predictive value (NPV) of 89.0%. Conservative patient-level later-positivity estimates were 10.8% within 12 weeks and 27.0% within 24 weeks, without same-lesion verification. This study supports the value of a deterministic pipeline for standardising imaging-derived response outputs in glioblastoma clinical trials. Future work will focus on prospective multi-institutional validation incorporating clinical variables, non-enhancing disease assessment, and adjudicated outcomes.

papers.abstract: Renal cancer is a fatal disease and ranks among the 14 common cancers in the latest WHO ranking. Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) prediction not only diagnoses the disease at early stages but also prevents patients from suffering pain and eventual death. This study aimed to construct and validate a model that predicts renal cancer using machine learning (ML) classifiers. Feature engineering techniques were used to refine the dataset, such as interaction feature generation, which categorizes the features according to values such as BMI, eGFR, and radiographic size. Binary clinical risk flags identify clinical risks according to the feature values, and correlation pruning removes the common and correlated features among various features. Three public datasets were collected, and the performance of seven machine learning classifiers was evaluated using the proposed model. The evaluation parameters included accuracy, precision, recall/sensitivity, specificity, F1 score, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC). An Explainable AI method was used to visualize the importance of the model characteristics. Among all the algorithms, the Multilevel Perceptron (MLP) algorithm fits best for the prediction of renal cancer with 98%, 96%, and 100% accuracy, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAPs) are used to visualize the importance of all model features. The proposed model provides an efficient method and shorter computation time to predict renal cancer using clinical features.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: In recent years, the number of cancer survivors has increased. Psychological difficulties or disorders are frequent during survivorship (e.g., fear of cancer recurrence, anxiety, depression, and insomnia). Various interventions have been developed to address survivors' specific psychosocial needs. This rapid scoping review aimed to define the interventions that have been developed for adult cancer survivors by describing (1) the type of intervention, (2) their measured psychosocial outcome variables, and (3) participants' main characteristics. Methods: PubMed was searched for articles published between 2020 and 2025. The search strategy combined terms related to cancer survivorship, psychosocial outcomes, and interventions. Titles and abstracts were screened, and data were extracted using a structured form specifying study type, population, intervention, and outcome characteristics. PRISMA-ScR guidelines were followed. Results: Out of 1743 screened studies, 80 were included (67 studies, 13 systematic reviews/meta-analyses), representing approximately 7880 cancer survivors (from the n = 67). Nearly 45% of included studies were conducted in the United States, and most interventions were developed for breast cancer survivors (38.8%) or included a majority of female participants. Physical activity (22.39%), psychoeducation (17.9%), and cognitive behavioural therapy (16.4%) were the most common intervention types. About a third incorporated eHealth or telehealth. Two-thirds of studies (65.7%) reported predominantly positive effects on psychosocial outcomes. Few interventions included cultural adaptations and targeted minority or socioeconomically disadvantaged populations. Conclusions: Most interventions for cancer survivors targeted breast cancer, female survivors in high-income countries. Developing and implementing culturally adapted and cost-efficient interventions, particularly for underrepresented survivor groups, remains a priority for future research and implementation.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Distant metastasis to the infratemporal fossa (ITF) is rare and can mimic primary skull-base tumors. We systematically reviewed reported distant ITF metastases. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 (PROSPERO CRD420261422546), PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched through 12 June 2026, for reports of ITF metastasis from a distant primary tumor; direct extension from adjacent tumors was excluded. Data were summarized descriptively, and reports were appraised with the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Case Reports. Results: Seventeen reports (17 patients) were included (median age 59 years). The lung was the most frequent primary site (n = 4), followed by the kidney, colorectum, and thyroid (n = 3 each); adenocarcinoma was the most common histology (n = 7). Facial pain (n = 9) and numbness (n = 6) predominated. Bone destruction was reported in 12 patients, and the maxillary sinus (n = 7), orbit (n = 6), pterygopalatine fossa (n = 5), middle cranial fossa (n = 5), and cavernous sinus (n = 4) were involved. The median reported interval to ITF metastasis was 36 months; 11 metastases were metachronous, and 11 patients had other metastatic disease during the reported course. Five patients underwent regional resection or debulking; radiotherapy was reported in eight, radioiodine in three, and systemic drug treatment in nine. At last follow-up, 11 patients were alive, four had died, and status was unknown in two. Conclusions: Distant ITF metastases may present with facial pain and cranial neuropathies. Prognosis is insufficiently characterized, and management should be individualized within a multidisciplinary team. The evidence is limited to case reports with incomplete reporting. No external funding was received.

papers.abstract: Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy worldwide and remains a major cause of cancer-related mortality among women. Despite advances in screening, molecular classification, and systemic therapies, treatment of advanced and metastatic disease remains challenging because of tumor heterogeneity, multidrug resistance, systemic toxicity, limited drug selectivity, and inadequate penetration into the tumor microenvironment. This review aims to critically evaluate advanced drug delivery systems (DDSs) for breast cancer therapy, emphasizing the relationship between carrier design, tumor biology, therapeutic performance, and clinical translation. The recent literature on DDSs for breast cancer treatment was comprehensively reviewed, covering liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles and micelles, dendrimers, nanogels, lipid- and inorganic-based nanoparticles, extracellular vesicles, biomimetic platforms, and stimuli-responsive systems. Particular attention was given to active and passive targeting, controlled drug release, strategies for overcoming multidrug resistance and biological barriers, and combination approaches integrating chemotherapy with immunotherapy, gene therapy, and phototherapy. Clinically approved and clinical-stage nanomedicines were also considered. Advanced DDSs can improve drug stability, pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, tumor accumulation, cellular uptake, and controlled release, potentially enhancing therapeutic efficacy while reducing systemic toxicity. Targeted, biomimetic, and stimuli-responsive platforms provide additional opportunities to address tumor heterogeneity, the tumor microenvironment, and therapeutic resistance. Several DDS-based nanomedicines have reached clinical use or advanced clinical development, demonstrating their translational potential. However, manufacturing scalability, reproducibility, long-term safety, regulatory requirements, and patient heterogeneity remain important barriers. Advanced DDSs represent promising tools for improving the precision and efficacy of breast cancer treatment. Future progress will require biologically informed carrier design, reproducible manufacturing, rigorous clinical validation, and patient stratification. Integrating nanomedicine with precision oncology may accelerate the clinical translation of next-generation DDSs and support more effective personalized therapeutic strategies.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Burkitt lymphoma (BL) is an aggressive germinal center B-cell (gcBC) malignancy driven by MYC deregulation and cooperating molecular alterations. A mouse model combining constitutive MYC and PI3K activity in gcBC closely recapitulates key features of human BL, but its epigenetic similarity to the human disease has not been investigated in detail. Here, we compared genome-wide DNA methylation patterns between human sporadic EBV-negative BL and this murine model. Methods: DNA methylation profiles of 37 human BL samples and 20 gcBC controls were compared with those of 8 murine tumors from the MYC/PI3K driven mouse model and 11 murine gcBC controls using Illumina methylation arrays. Differentially methylated CpGs were identified using linear modeling, and chromatin-state enrichment, cross-species gene overlap, protein interaction, and pathway enrichment analyses were performed. Results: BL showed global DNA hypomethylation in both species and distinct methylation profiles from gcBCs. CpGs hypomethylated in BL were enriched at enhancers, whereas hypermethylated CpGs were strongly enriched at poised promoters. We identified 695 genes with shared hypermethylation and 512 with shared hypomethylation between human and murine BL. Restricting the analysis to regulatory regions identified 86 genes consistently hypomethylated in both species. These genes were significantly enriched for regulation of intracellular signal transduction and sphingolipid signaling. Included are regulators of GTPase and kinase signaling, such as GNA13, RASA3, RASAL1, SPRED2, PIK3R2, PRKCA, PRKCE, and FYN. The conserved set also contained genes with established roles in germinal center B-cell biology, including FOXO1, BACH2, and NR3C1. Conclusions: Human and murine BL share conserved regulatory DNA methylation features, supporting the MYC/PI3K mouse model as a system to study epigenetic mechanisms of BL.

papers.abstract: Background/Hypothesis: Therapeutic resistance and recurrence remain major barriers to durable cancer control because conventional therapies may eliminate proliferating tumor cells while allowing dormant, stem-like, senescence-like, or polyploid populations to persist. This review examines polyploid giant cancer cells (PGCCs) as therapy-tolerant states and evaluates whether their adaptive survival mechanisms create vulnerabilities that could be targeted through ferroptosis-oriented nanomedicine. Methods: We investigated recent evidence (PubMed) linking PGCC persistence with redox buffering, glutathione/GPX4 activity, iron regulation, lipid remodeling, autophagy, mitochondrial adaptation, and metabolic plasticity, in addition to nanomedicine potential to target these pathways. Results and Findings: Emerging studies provide direct proof-of-concept that PGCCs can exhibit ferroptosis susceptibility, while nanomedicine offers potential strategies to improve therapeutic localization and coordinate iron delivery, reactive oxygen species amplification, glutathione depletion, GPX4 inhibition, and combination therapy. However, PGCC-selective nanoparticle efficacy remains largely untested, and important barriers include heterogeneous tumor penetration, off-target toxicity, model limitations, and biomarker uncertainty. Conclusions and Perspective: The specific contribution of this review is to integrate PGCC biology, therapy-tolerant cancer states, ferroptosis, and nanomedicine into a unified framework for targeting residual disease. This perspective is timely as direct evidence of PGCC ferroptosis sensitivity and new characterization of treatment-resistant PGCC states are emerging. By identifying the mechanistic overlap among these fields, this review highlights testable opportunities for eliminating persistent cancer cells that may otherwise contribute to recurrence.

papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Cutaneous melanoma spreads preferentially through the lymphatic system, and sentinel lymph node status is among the strongest prognostic factors. Whether tumour angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis add prognostic information beyond conventional histopathology has been examined in many immunohistochemical studies, with heterogeneous results. We conducted a systematic review, reported according to PRISMA 2020 and not registered, of blood microvascular density (MVD), lymphatic vessel density (LVD) in the intratumoral and peritumoral compartments, proliferating (Ki-67-positive) lymphatic vessels and lymphatic invasion (LI) as prognostic markers in primary cutaneous melanoma. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE was searched to 10 September 2026, supplemented by a Web of Science export and by citation tracking of the reference meta-analysis by Pastushenko et al. (2014). Twenty-one cutaneous study units (25 reports) and four ocular studies providing indirect evidence were included, and risk of bias was rated with the QUIPS tool. Results: In the reference meta-analysis, peritumoral LVD and LI, but not MVD or intratumoral LVD, were associated with metastasis. The newer cohorts confirmed this pattern and provided adjusted effect sizes: peritumoral LVD predicted disease-free (HR 2.14) and melanoma-specific survival (HR of 2.74; 95% CI 1.31 to 5.73), immunohistochemically detected LI predicted sentinel node metastasis (33% vs. 11% positive nodes) and overall survival, and a Ki-67-positive lymphatic endothelium predicted melanoma-specific mortality (adjusted HR of 2.03; 95% CI 1.33 to 3.10) in 264 patients. Blood MVD and blood endothelial proliferation were not prognostic. Heterogeneity of markers, counting methods and effect measures precluded re-pooling. Conclusions: Peritumoral LVD, LI and proliferating lymphatics are promising adjunct biomarkers for selecting patients for sentinel node biopsy, adjuvant therapy and closer follow-up, pending standardised, digital-pathology-based quantification.

papers.abstract: High tertiary lymphoid structure (TLS) density predicts favorable outcomes in several solid tumors but worse outcomes in bladder cancer, and the basis for this discrepancy is unclear. In this issue, Péricart and colleagues leverage en bloc resection of non-muscle-invasive bladder tumors to show that TLS accumulate without acquiring the features of productive antitumor immunity. The work reframes TLS in this setting as structures for which functional state, not abundance, dictates their contribution to tumor control. See related article by Péricart et al., p. XX.
